title: Should bodybuilders care about strength?
summary: NH argues bodybuilders should care about strength, not as an end but as the most objective trainable measure of progress and a byproduct of hypertrophy. Strength exists across rep ranges and is rep-range specific, progressive overload takes many forms, and bodybuilders should train both lower and higher rep ranges because each drives the other.

claims.claim: Strength doesn't strictly correlate with size between individuals (bigger legs don't guarantee a bigger squat).
For a natural bodybuilder, strength is the most objective value to program around and assess progress, after body measurements; how you look in the mirror trumps all.
You needn't obsess over new numbers, but progression on your lifts equals progression for your muscles.
Treat strength as a byproduct of hypertrophy: taking strict EZ-bar curls from 60 to 100 lbs for 6 reps will grow your biceps.
Some people gain strength faster than size, but a large percentage strength gain on a lift without any muscle adaptation is biologically impossible.
Structure sessions by opening with strength-focused lifts, then follow with more volume at less strength-focused rep ranges.
Strength isn't only found in low reps, but specificity applies: if you only train high reps, rep-max calculators overestimate your 1RM, and vice versa for low-rep lifters.
NH has always been better at higher rep ranges than explosive one-rep maxes; this depends on training and muscle fiber type.
Bodybuilders who say 'ignore the weight, focus on feel' either misunderstand natural physiology or apply progressive overload unknowingly.
Progressive overload can be more weight, shorter rest between sets, slower tempo, or supersetting with another exercise.
Bodybuilders care about what the weight does to the muscle, not the weight itself; if two plates built big legs he would squat two plates, but below a threshold load stops stimulating.
Bodybuilders need both lower and higher rep ranges; the exact ranges are personal preference.
NH never does singles, doubles or triples on certain lifts and never goes above 15 reps.
Raising your 10RM on a bench variation raises your 4RM and vice versa; sticking to one range makes you overly specific and leads to plateaus.
High-rep-only training stalls eventually; heavier lower-rep work shocks the muscle and later lets you move more weight for more reps, increasing tonnage.
Reach strength numbers to help your body grow, not for their own sake; this broad mentality prevents plateaus and mental burnout.
